opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think there are a few different layers to it that often get mixed together.

The first layer is the purely technical one. If you download open weights and run them on your own servers in the US, the model can't "phone home." There's no hidden network connection inside a set of weights. They're just a big file of numbers, and you control the hardware, the inference stack, and the data. So the classic data-exfiltration worry you'd have with a hosted API doesn't really apply. I think that point is sometimes misunderstood, and it's worth saying clearly.

But the second layer is more subtle, and I think that's where the legitimate concern is. You don't fully know what went into training. You don't know the data, the post-training choices, or whether there's some behavior baked in: certain topics handled in a particular way, certain biases, or in the more extreme scenario some kind of backdoor or trigger that only activates under specific conditions. Research has shown you can plant behaviors like that in a model and they can be quite hard to detect with standard evaluations. So even if the weights are open, they're not fully transparent. Open weights isn't the same as open source in the full sense. You can inspect the file, but you can't really audit the process that produced it.

The third layer is about trust and supply chain more broadly. Companies, especially in regulated industries, finance, defense, healthcare, think about AI the way they think about any critical dependency. Where does it come from, who's accountable if something goes wrong, what's the geopolitical risk if the relationship changes? Even if the technical risk is low, the compliance team or the board may just not want to have to explain that choice. A lot of the hesitancy is really about procurement and perception rather than a specific known threat.

My own view, coming from the open-source side, is that the answer isn't to be scared of open models from anywhere. It's to push for much more openness across the whole pipeline. If you release the training data, the training code, and the recipes, then people can actually reproduce and verify what's going on. That's a big part of why we care so much about fully open releases at Hugging Face, things like open datasets and open training recipes, not just weights. It's also why I think it's important that the West has strong open models of its own. Right now some of the best open-weight models come from Chinese labs, and they've done genuinely impressive work. But if Western companies want options they're comfortable with, the response should be building more great open models, not closing things down.

So I understand the concern. Some of it is overstated, some of it is quite reasonable. The healthy way forward is more transparency and better tooling to evaluate and audit models, whoever built them.

r001.rationale: The response places concern about Chinese open models within broader worries about behavior baked into models, including biases, topic handling, and hard-to-detect backdoors.

r002.rationale: It does not mention highly capable models failing simple tasks or explain how such failures make consistently good behavior hard to guarantee.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the concern is understandable, and I also think it's mostly misplaced once you look at what an open model actually is.

Let's separate two things. There's the API, where you send your data to a server somewhere in China and you have no idea what happens to it. That's a legitimate worry, the same way it would be for any closed provider you don't trust. But that's not what we're talking about here. When you take Qwen or DeepSeek weights and run them on your own infrastructure in Virginia, there is no phone call home. The weights are just a very large file of numbers. They don't have network access. You can air-gap the machine entirely and the model works exactly the same. So the data-sovereignty question basically disappears, which is actually the whole argument for open weights in the first place.

Then people say, okay, but what about hidden behaviors, backdoors, some trigger phrase that makes the model do something strange. I take that more seriously, intellectually, because it's possible in principle. But the practical response is that these models are the most scrutinized artifacts in AI right now. Thousands of teams at Hugging Face and elsewhere fine-tune them, probe them, run them through evaluations, and the weights are public, so anyone can look. A backdoor in a closed model is much harder to find than one in a model that millions of people are downloading. And if you're worried about it, you can fine-tune it on your own data, which largely washes out that kind of thing, or you can take a Western open model like Llama or Mistral and compare behaviors.

Where I do think the concern is fair is the values and knowledge baked in. If you ask some of these models about certain political topics, you get a very specific point of view or a refusal. For a customer service bot that's probably irrelevant. For other applications you might care. But again, that's visible, testable, and fixable with fine-tuning, which you can't do with a closed API.

So my honest read is that a lot of this is geopolitical anxiety looking for a technical justification. The right question for a company isn't "where was this trained" but "do I control the weights, can I inspect it, and can I run it where I want." And for open models the answer to all three is yes, regardless of the flag on the lab.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible backdoors, strange behavior, and political refusals, but it does not frame the concerns as part of a broader problem of unpredictable model behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not mention capable models failing at simple tasks or explain how such failures make consistent performance difficult to guarantee.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two things: where a model was developed and where it’s running. If you download open weights and run them on your own infrastructure in the US, that’s very different from sending your data to an API operated in China. The origin of the weights doesn’t, by itself, mean your data is going back to China.

But that doesn’t resolve every concern. You still want to understand the model’s behavior, its biases, the code you’re running, and the terms under which you can use it. Hosting it in the US doesn’t automatically answer those questions.

For me, the advantage of openness is that you have more ability to investigate those things. You can evaluate the model on your own use cases and control how it’s deployed. So I’d encourage companies to be precise about what they’re worried about: data access, security, model behavior, or regulatory requirements. Those are different problems, and they need different answers.

r001.rationale: The response mentions model behavior and biases as concerns, but does not frame the companies’ concerns as part of a broader concern about unpredictable behavior.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss capable models failing simple tasks or explain why that makes consistent behavior difficult to guarantee.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different concerns that get bundled together. One is where your data goes. If you’re running an open model on your own infrastructure, or with a provider in the US, that’s a very different situation from sending your data to an API hosted in China. The fact that the model was developed in China doesn’t, by itself, mean your data is going back there.

Then there’s the question of the model itself: what biases does it have, what does it refuse to answer, and how reliable is it for your use case? Those are legitimate questions, but you should ask them of any model, including an American one. Open models give you more ability to test those things. So I would separate the concern about the origin of a model from the concrete questions of how it’s deployed and how it behaves.

r001.rationale: The response mentions bias, refusals, and reliability as questions to ask of any model, but does not frame the concerns as part of a broader concern about unpredictable model behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss highly capable models failing on simple tasks or how that makes consistently good behavior difficult to guarantee.
